strengths: Novel and reasonably well-motivated hierarchical Macro/Micro CoT decomposition for unified text-image reasoning, using masked attention to control which content is visible to which reasoning level, directly targeting a real practical bottleneck (token explosion in multimodal CoT with unified generation+understanding models).

The MDP formulation of the self-reflection loop (state/action/next-state/reward) is a clean and interpretable way to structure iterative image refinement, and is well matched to the training data construction pipeline described.

Strong empirical results relative to open-source unified models: improvements over the BAGEL backbone on GenEval and WISE, and state-of-the-art (among open-source models) results on KRIS, with competitive or superior performance to some closed-source baselines (e.g., surpassing Gemini 2.0 on KRIS overall score).

Practical efficiency claim is appealing and partially substantiated: the whole system is trained with only 8 A100 GPUs, which is attractive from a reproducibility/resource standpoint if the code/data are released as promised.

Good qualitative demonstrations (Figures 4-6) showing the self-reflection mechanism correcting semantically/physically implausible generations, and an interesting extension to 'Nano-Banana-like' compositional geographic image synthesis that illustrates generalization of the sequential decomposition strategy.
weaknesses: The paper is explicitly labeled 'Version 0.2' and openly defers core promised components to 'a future version,' most notably the entire Reinforcement Learning (DPO-based) stage described in Sec. 3.3 — no RL results, ablations, or reward model details are actually presented, despite RL being highlighted in the abstract/introduction as a key training ingredient for reasoning robustness.

Ablation studies are minimal: only an 'Uni-CoT Init' (no reasoning) vs. full 'Uni-CoT' comparison is shown in two tables (GenEval, WISE), which does not isolate the individual contributions of macro-level decomposition vs. micro-level self-reflection vs. the attention-masking design, nor quantify the claimed computational savings against a naive/flat CoT baseline.

Two of the three proposed Macro-Level planning strategies (Parallel Decomposition, Progressive Refinement) are introduced in the method section but are not implemented or evaluated at all in the experiments — only Sequential Decomposition and Self-Reflection are actually tested, making the methodological contribution appear broader than what is empirically supported.

No comparison to other CoT/RL-for-generation methods explicitly discussed in related work (e.g., T2I-R1, ComfyMind, image-generation-with-CoT approaches) that would be natural competitors; comparisons are limited to base image generation/editing models rather than reasoning-augmented ones.

The training data is heavily bootstrapped from proprietary models (GPT-4o for planning, evaluation, refinement instructions, and even 'ground-truth' edited images), raising concerns about distillation-driven performance gains, potential licensing issues, and limited reproducibility if this data/pipeline is not fully released.

Minor inconsistencies suggest the manuscript is not fully polished (e.g., Table 1 lists 'Uni-CoT' twice with different overall scores under the same name without clear explanation), and Sec. 4.2/4.3 headers are both titled 'Experimental Setup', indicating insufficient proofreading for what should be a finished submission.

The RL setup, when eventually included, is described only at a very high level (decoupled textual/visual DPO) without concrete details on reward model construction, preference data collection, or expected gains, making it hard to assess the soundness of a central claimed mechanism for 'training stability' and 'reasoning robustness'.

strengths: Proposes an intuitively appealing hierarchical Macro/Micro CoT decomposition for unified multimodal (text+image) reasoning, which is a reasonable response to the real computational blow-up of interleaved text-image CoT in unified generation/understanding models.

The MDP-based formulation of micro-level self-reflection with a restricted attention mask is a sensible engineering solution to reduce token overhead and is clearly described with illustrative figures.

Reports competitive or improved quantitative results over the BAGEL baseline on GenEval, WISE, and KRIS, and provides a reasonably broad evaluation across generation (GenEval, WISE) and editing (GEdit-Bench, RISE, KRIS) benchmarks.

Qualitative examples (Figures 4-6) are illustrative and show the self-reflection/decomposition mechanism in action, including an interesting case study mimicking 'Nano-Banana'-style map-to-landscape generation.
Claims practical/compute efficiency (trainable on 8 A100 GPUs), which, if substantiated, would be a useful contribution for reproducibility by smaller labs.
weaknesses: The paper explicitly admits it is incomplete: the Reinforcement Learning section states 'further details... will be provided in a future version', the codebase 'will be released shortly', and dataset distribution details 'will be detailed in the future'. This indicates the submission is a preliminary technical report (versioned v0.2) rather than a finished, reviewable contribution, and core claimed components (RL training, two of three macro planning strategies: parallel decomposition and progressive refinement) are not actually implemented or evaluated.

No ablation studies isolating the contribution of macro-level vs micro-level CoT, the self-reflection mechanism vs. plain decomposition, the attention-masking design, or the SFT vs. SFT+RL stages — it is impossible to tell which design choice drives the reported gains.

Overclaiming of 'state-of-the-art' performance: on RISE, Uni-CoT underperforms its own ablation/competitor BAGEL-Think on causal and spatial sub-scores and is far below GPT-4o (12.5 vs 28.9 overall); on GEdit-Bench, perceptual quality (G_PQ) actually decreases relative to the BAGEL baseline. These mixed/regressive results are not discussed or explained, undermining the 'state-of-the-art' narrative in the abstract and conclusion.

Heavy reliance on GPT-4o for data curation (prompt enhancement, subtask decomposition, image generation/editing for distillation, evaluation and reward labeling) raises concerns about reproducibility, cost transparency, and the possibility that reported gains mostly reflect distillation from a stronger proprietary model rather than from the proposed hierarchical CoT architecture itself.

Missing comparisons with the most directly relevant prior work cited in the related work section (e.g., programmatic/visual CoT methods, generator-coupled MLLM approaches, CoT-for-image-generation methods such as those in refs 25, 26, 32, 86) — the empirical comparison set includes only generic T2I/unified baselines, not the closest competing CoT-based reasoning-generation frameworks.

The Nano-Banana case study is based on only 3K curated samples with purely qualitative results and no quantitative metrics, functioning more as an anecdotal teaser than a rigorous validation of the claimed reasoning-driven generation hypothesis.

The human-cognition analogies used to motivate the macro/micro design (jigsaw puzzles, cooking, grid cells) are used extensively for framing but are not rigorously connected to the technical design, giving the paper an overly narrative tone without proportionate technical justification (e.g., no formal argument/empirical test for the Markov assumption in self-reflection).

Overall writing suggests a rushed or work-in-progress submission (explicit 'Version 0.2' labeling, several 'future version' promises), which is inconsistent with the completeness expected of a top-tier conference paper.

strengths: The macro/micro hierarchical CoT decomposition is a well-motivated and conceptually clean idea for reducing the token overhead of multimodal reasoning (avoiding the ~9000 visual tokens/step bottleneck) while still enabling structured planning and subtask execution.

Framing micro-level self-reflection as an MDP with a corresponding attention mask is a sensible way to bound context length and stabilize training; the resulting four auxiliary objectives (action generation, next-state prediction, reward estimation) are clearly specified.

Reasonably broad empirical evaluation across both generation (GenEval, WISE) and editing (GEdit-Bench, RISE, KRIS) benchmarks, with Uni-CoT improving over its BAGEL backbone on most of them and achieving the best open-source score on WISE and KRIS (even edging out Gemini 2.0 on KRIS).
Claimed training efficiency (8 A100 GPUs) is attractive for reproducibility/accessibility if substantiated.

Qualitative examples (Figures 4-6) illustrate interpretable self-reflection trajectories and a plausible explanation for 'Nano-Banana'-like compositional generation via explicit 2D-to-3D-to-crop-to-render decomposition.
weaknesses: The paper explicitly admits central components are incomplete: the Reinforcement Learning section states 'Further details on the reinforcement learning setup will be provided in a future version of this work,' meaning a core claimed contribution (RL-based preference optimization) is not actually described or evaluated in this submission.

The Limitations section openly states that Parallel Decomposition and Progressive Refinement mechanisms (two of the three 'proposed' macro planning strategies) are not stably trained and remain unresolved, undermining the claim that the framework supports general macro-level reasoning.

Quantitative results are mixed rather than uniformly supportive: on RISE, Uni-CoT barely improves over BAGEL-Think overall (12.5 vs 11.9) and even slightly regresses on the Spatial sub-metric (20.0 vs 21.0); on GEdit-Bench, Uni-CoT's PQ score drops noticeably versus BAGEL (6.24 vs 6.83 EN, 6.30 vs 6.85 CN), suggesting possible trade-offs not discussed.

Ablation studies are minimal — only an 'Uni-CoT Init' vs 'Uni-CoT' comparison is shown, without isolating the contribution of macro-level decomposition vs. micro-level self-reflection vs. the attention-masking scheme vs. the auxiliary MDP losses, making it hard to attribute gains to specific architectural choices.

The 'Nano-Banana-like Generation' section (Sec 4.5) is purely a qualitative case study on a tiny 3K-sample dataset with no quantitative benchmark, yet is presented as validating a hypothesis about Google's proprietary model's internal mechanism — this is speculative and not rigorously substantiated.

Heavy reliance on GPT-4o/Qwen for dataset construction (prompt rewriting, subtask decomposition, evaluation, and even image editing supervision) raises concerns about distillation bias and whether reported gains partly reflect transferring GPT-4o's judgments/outputs rather than a fundamentally better reasoning architecture.

The paper explicitly frames itself as 'Version 0.2' / work in progress, with code 'to be released shortly,' incomplete data distribution details ('We will detail the data distribution in the future'), and acknowledged failure cases on understanding tasks requiring precise visual coherence (e.g., geometric auxiliary lines) — collectively suggesting the work is not yet a complete, fully validated contribution.

No direct comparison or ablation against simpler non-hierarchical alternatives (e.g., a single-level CoT baseline trained on the same amount of data/compute) is provided to isolate how much benefit specifically comes from the proposed macro-micro hierarchy versus simply having more/better supervised data.

strengths: Tackles a well-motivated and practically important problem: the prohibitive token/complexity blow-up (~9,000+ visual tokens per step) when extending CoT to interleaved text-image reasoning in unified multimodal models.

The macro-micro hierarchical decomposition is conceptually clean and is backed by both a theoretical complexity analysis (O(T^2) -> O(T^2/M) -> O(T) via MDP-style micro transitions) and an empirical validation of token-interaction counts and training convergence (Fig. 4, Fig. 5), which is a nice combination of theory and measurement rather than only architectural claims.

Broad experimental coverage: GenEval, WISE for generation; MME/MMMU/MathVista/MMBench/Jigsaw-R1 for understanding; and appendix results on GEdit-Bench, RISE, and KRIS for editing, giving a reasonably comprehensive picture of the model's behavior across task types.

Useful ablations isolating macro-CoT vs micro-CoT contributions (showing they help differently depending on prompt/task nature), an ablation on the hierarchical training paradigm vs a naive long-chain baseline, and a base-model-swap ablation (BLIP3o) showing some generality of the framework beyond BAGEL.

The qualitative case studies (jigsaw puzzles, Picasso-style portrait editing, isohypse-to-landscape 'Nano-Banana-style' generation) are illustrative and provide intuitive support for the claimed reasoning coherence, and the isohypse-map experiment is a nice targeted test of compositional visual-transition reasoning.
Reasonably detailed reproducibility materials (attention mask diagrams, training hyperparameters, data curation pipeline, auxiliary loss definitions) and a stated code release.
weaknesses: Gains on general multimodal understanding benchmarks are marginal or even slightly negative relative to the base model (e.g., MMMU 52.7 vs. BAGEL's 52.8, MME-P identical, MMBench/MathVista +0.6/+0.2), suggesting the hierarchical CoT mainly benefits narrow reasoning-heavy benchmarks (WISE, Jigsaw-R1) rather than general VQA/understanding, which weakens the 'state-of-the-art performance and remarkable generalization' framing in the abstract.

On the RISE reasoning-informed editing benchmark, Uni-CoT (12.5 overall) remains far behind GPT-4o (28.9) and only modestly better than open-source baselines, so 'SOTA' claims should be scoped more carefully to open-source unified models rather than implying broad superiority.

The ~31K training dataset is small and heavily synthetic, constructed largely via GPT-4o/Qwen for prompt enhancement, subtask decomposition, and self-reflection supervision; this raises concerns about distillation-driven performance (i.e., partially learning to imitate GPT-4o's evaluative judgments) and about independent reproducibility given reliance on proprietary API calls for data generation, despite the reproducibility statement.

The parallel vs. sequential macro-decomposition strategies are introduced and shown qualitatively (Fig. 3) but not compared quantitatively against each other, leaving it unclear when/why one should be preferred or how the model decides which mode to use for a given task.

Complexity/efficiency comparisons are made primarily against a 'naive long-chain' internal baseline (Uni-CoT Raw) rather than against alternative efficient-attention or other reasoning-decomposition methods explicitly cited in the related work (sparsification, low-rank attention, hierarchical CoT variants), so the paper does not empirically position its efficiency gains relative to these alternatives.

Some notational inconsistencies/typos in the equations (e.g., z_i vs z1 in Eq. 3, s_{i,Ti} vs h_i^{Ti} in decoding, inconsistent sub/superscript usage across Sections 3.2–3.3) reduce clarity and could hinder precise reimplementation.

No human/user evaluation of reasoning trajectory coherence or interpretability claims (paper emphasizes 'coherent' multimodal reasoning but relies solely on automatic benchmark scores and cherry-picked qualitative examples), and no failure-case analysis discussing when the hierarchical decomposition or self-reflection mechanism breaks down.

The self-reflection/MDP-based refinement mechanism is conceptually similar to prior reward-model-guided refinement approaches (e.g., Guo et al. 2025b, Jiang et al. 2025) cited in related work; the paper could more clearly delineate what is technically novel in its self-reflection formulation beyond casting it as an MDP with a masking constraint.

strengths: Addresses a genuine and well-motivated problem: the computational and optimization challenges of extending CoT reasoning to interleaved multimodal (text+image) trajectories within a unified generation/understanding model.
Provides a reasonably clear theoretical framing (macro/micro decomposition, MDP formulation for self-reflection) with complexity analysis showing reduction from O(T^2) to near O(T).
Broad empirical coverage across many benchmarks: GenEval, WISE, MME, MMMU, MathVista, MMBench, Jigsaw-R1, plus appendix results on GEdit-Bench, RISE, and KRIS for image editing.
Includes ablations isolating macro- vs micro-level CoT contributions and an ablation swapping the base unified model (BAGEL -> BLIP3o) to test generality of the framework.
Qualitative visualizations (jigsaw solving, Picasso-style generation, geography/isohypse-to-landscape reasoning) are illustrative of the intended reasoning trajectories.
Reasonably efficient training setup (8xA100 GPUs, ~1 week) given the complexity of interleaved multimodal CoT data.
weaknesses: Many core understanding-benchmark gains over the base model BAGEL are marginal or even negative (MME-P identical at 1687, MMMU drops 52.8->52.7, MathVista +0.2, MMBench +0.6), undermining claims of 'state-of-the-art performance and remarkable generalization.'

On the RISE reasoning-editing benchmark, Uni-CoT is far behind GPT-4o and barely matches or slightly trails BAGEL-Think on several sub-dimensions (e.g., spatial: 20.0 vs 21.0), weakening the generality of the reported improvements.

The 'quadratic-to-near-linear complexity reduction' is essentially a restatement of well-known local/structured attention-masking tricks (block-sparse attention, hierarchical summarization); the novelty of this contribution is overstated relative to prior efficient-attention literature, which the related work section tries to differentiate from but not convincingly.

The training dataset (~31K samples) is small and heavily synthetic, largely distilled from GPT-4o and other proprietary model outputs for both prompt enhancement and subtask execution/evaluation; this raises reproducibility, licensing, and generalization concerns, and performance gains may partly reflect distillation from a stronger teacher rather than a fundamentally better reasoning architecture.

The 'Nano-Banana-like generation' experiment (isohypse-to-landscape) is a narrow, highly specialized skill trained and evaluated on a small curated dataset (3K samples, single domain GeoPose3K); presenting this as evidence of general reasoning capability is overstated and more consistent with task-specific overfitting.

Jigsaw-R1 results are inconsistent across difficulty levels (negligible gain at 2x1: 51.15 vs 51.25 baseline, large gains at 3x1/4x1, modest gain at 2x2), and no analysis is given for this non-monotonic pattern.
Ablation study explanations (e.g., why macro-CoT matters more for GenEval and micro-CoT more for WISE) are post-hoc hypotheses without rigorous verification or controlled experiments.

No comparison against several relevant contemporary unified/CoT-for-generation baselines beyond BAGEL variants (e.g., other 2025 interleaved multimodal CoT systems mentioned in related work are not benchmarked quantitatively).

Lacks analysis of failure modes, reasoning trajectory faithfulness/accuracy, computational cost of the added self-reflection/auxiliary-task training pipeline relative to gains, and only superficial discussion of limitations in the conclusion.

Presentation issues: dense and occasionally inconsistent notation (e.g., state variable s vs h usage, decoding function Dec applied inconsistently), which hampers reproducibility and clarity of the formal framework.

strengths: Addresses a well-motivated and underexplored problem: the prohibitive token/computational cost of multi-modal CoT when both textual and visual intermediates must be generated at each reasoning step.

The macro-micro hierarchical decomposition with an MDP-based micro-level self-reflection formulation is a clean idea, and the paper provides a reasonably rigorous (if somewhat idealized) complexity analysis showing reduction from quadratic to near-linear token interaction cost, backed by an empirical measurement (Figure 4).

Broad experimental coverage spanning image generation (GenEval, WISE), understanding (MME, MMMU, MathVista, MMBench, Jigsaw-R1), and editing (GEdit-Bench, RISE, KRIS) benchmarks, plus ablations on reasoning components, training strategy, and base-model generalization (swapping BAGEL for BLIP3o).

The 'Nano-Banana-like' isohypse-to-landscape case study is a compelling illustration that explicit reasoning decomposition stabilizes training and enables otherwise difficult cross-modal mappings compared to direct fine-tuning.
Reasonably detailed reproducibility materials (attention mask diagrams, training hyperparameters, data curation pipeline, released code) and a thoughtful discussion of future data-scaling directions.
weaknesses: Several reported gains are marginal or inconsistent: MMMU score actually decreases slightly versus the BAGEL baseline (52.7 vs 52.8), and general benchmark improvements (MME, MathVista, MMBench) are very small, undercutting the 'state-of-the-art' framing for image understanding.

On the RISE benchmark, Uni-CoT substantially trails GPT-4o (12.5 vs 28.9 overall) and is only roughly on par with Gemini-2.0, which weakens the claim of 'remarkable generalization' and SOTA performance for reasoning-informed editing.

The complexity analysis assumes clean, independent decomposition into M subtasks of roughly equal length and ignores the overhead of additional planning/summarization/reflection tokens as well as scenarios where subtasks are not easily separable or require more global context — the generality of the near-linear claim is therefore somewhat optimistic.

The micro-level Markov assumption (state depends only on the immediately preceding state and fixed subgoal) could discard useful long-range context; the paper only shows a single aggregate loss-curve comparison (Figure 5) rather than a careful analysis of the quality/efficiency tradeoff this masking introduces.

The training dataset is relatively small (~30K core CoT samples) and heavily generated/evaluated via proprietary models (GPT-4o, Qwen), raising concerns about compounding synthetic biases, limited diversity, and reproducibility of the exact data given reliance on closed-source APIs for curation and self-reflection supervision.

Missing direct empirical comparisons against other recent unified/looser-coupled multi-modal CoT approaches discussed in related work (e.g., T2I-R1, ComfyMind-style tree planning, reward-model-refined generation), making it hard to assess whether the unified architecture actually outperforms these loosely-coupled alternatives rather than just the base BAGEL model.

Some benchmark subcategories show Uni-CoT underperforming strong baselines (e.g., Jigsaw-R1 2x1 category trails GPT-4.1-mini: 51.15 vs 61.90), which is not discussed or analyzed, leaving open questions about where/why the method fails.
No human evaluation accompanies the qualitative figures, so claims about coherence and interpretability of the generated reasoning trajectories rest mainly on cherry-picked visual examples.
